name: archify
tagline: Describe a system in plain English and your AI agent draws an interactive diagram you can click, trace and export
sentence: Tell your AI coding agent what your system looks like - or point it at a codebase - and it builds a clickable, animated architecture map you can open in any browser.

board.say: You need to show people how your system works, but hand-drawn diagrams go stale the moment the code changes.
board.eg: The architecture slide from last quarter no longer matches what is actually running.

board.say: You describe the system in plain English - or point your AI agent at the code and say 'draw this'.
board.eg: 'Browser goes to API, API checks Redis cache, falls back to PostgreSQL.'

board.say: The agent turns your description into a structured blueprint, validates it, and renders an interactive map.
board.eg: It checks that every connection has two ends, then draws the diagram with clickable nodes and animated paths.

board.say: You get a single HTML file you can open in any browser - click nodes for details, trace paths, switch themes, export to PNG.
board.eg: No account, no server, no subscription. Send the file to a colleague and they see the same interactive map.

before: Architecture diagrams are static images that go out of date the moment someone changes the code.
Drawing a diagram by hand takes an afternoon; updating it when the system changes takes another.
Tools like Visio or Lucidchart need a subscription and produce flat images with no interactivity.
after: Say **"draw the architecture"** and your AI agent produces an interactive diagram in seconds.
Click any component to see its details, trace a path between two services, or play an animated walkthrough.
The output is one HTML file - no server, no account, no subscription. Open it in any browser and share it by email.
uses_note: About 5 months old, growing very fast. Mostly used by developers and architects to explain systems to teammates.

steps: Install the skill: run `npx skills add tt-a1i/archify -g` in your terminal.
Open your AI agent (Claude Code, Cursor, etc.) and say: 'Use archify to draw: Browser goes to API, API checks Redis, falls back to PostgreSQL.'
Open the HTML file it creates in your browser - click any node, press R to trace a route, press T to switch themes.
try.paste:
/skillspector https://github.com/tt-a1i/archify

If that scan passes: install the skill (`npx skills add tt-a1i/archify -g`), then use archify to draw this system: Browser -> API -> Redis cache -> PostgreSQL fallback. Open the HTML output and test the interactive features. 10 minutes max.

best_for: You want to explain a system to someone without drawing a diagram by hand
You need an architecture map that teammates can click and explore, not just look at
skip_if: You need diagrams inside GitHub README files (these are interactive HTML files, not Markdown-compatible)
You want to hand-draw or drag-and-drop your diagrams - this is AI-generated from descriptions
You need UML-standard diagrams for compliance or formal documentation

alternatives.name: Mermaid.js
alternatives.line: Text-based diagrams that render natively inside GitHub and GitLab. Static output, but works everywhere Markdown does.

alternatives.name: D2 (Terrastruct)
alternatives.line: Modern diagram-as-code language with clean syntax and good auto-layout. Static output, no AI agent integration.

watch: **Still rough around the edges.** One tester found 3 of 5 packaged examples fail archify's own validation check (issue #324). Start with simple diagrams and treat the output as a draft.
**No GitHub Markdown rendering.** The output is an interactive HTML file, not a Mermaid diagram. It will not render inside a README or a pull request description.
**Rapid star growth.** 0 to 72K stars in 5 months is unusually fast. Active development (105 commits/month) and real independent reviews suggest genuine adoption, but the pattern warrants attention.
